transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I, um... I've been debating whether or not I actually needed to come in, to be perfectly honest with you. My days are usually pretty quiet now that I'm not working anymore, and I try to keep myself occupied, you know, reading my books or just tending to the house. I've always been a fairly steady person. 

But lately... well, it's the mornings. The mornings have become just so strange and difficult. I'll open my eyes and look at the clock, and the sun is coming through the blinds—just like it always does, nothing has changed about my bedroom or my routine—but I just lie there. And... what really scared me, what actually made me finally pick up the phone and make this appointment, is that I keep having these mornings where I just lie in bed and think... I think it might just be easier if I didn't wake up at all. 

Now, I want to be very, very clear with you, I don't have a plan to hurt myself. I would never do that. I don't have any intention of doing anything drastic, I really don't. But just having that thought float into my head, that it would be so much simpler to just slip away in my sleep and not have to face the day... it really frightened me. It's just not like me to think that way, and it's been happening enough that I thought, well, I need to come in and talk to someone about this, because it's quite unsettling to not even want to get out of bed to live your life.
How long have you been experiencing these difficult mornings with thoughts about not wanting to wake up?

Well, let me think about that. It hasn't been forever, though sometimes when you're just lying there in the quiet, time sort of stretches out, you know? But if I really look at the calendar, I'd say it's been... yes, it's been about a month now. 

You see, it all started right around the time my sister passed away. And it was just... it was so incredibly unexpected. We were always very close—she was only two years older than me, and we talked on the phone almost every single evening. She lived just a couple of towns over, so we'd usually see each other for lunch on Tuesdays. We had our little routines. And then, completely out of nowhere... she was gone. One minute she was perfectly fine, and the next... well. It was a terrible shock. Just terrible. 

I had to help with a lot of the arrangements, you know, calling people and sorting through her things because her children live all the way out on the West Coast, so I was running on pure adrenaline for those first few days. I was just doing what needed to be done. But then, after the service, when everyone went back to their own lives and my house got quiet again... that's when these mornings really started. So, yes, it's been about four weeks, ever since she died, that I've been waking up and just having those awful thoughts about how much easier it would be to just stay asleep.
Do you find yourself enjoying the things you used to like, such as reading or spending time with others, as much as you did before your sister passed away?

Well, that's... that's a very good question, Doctor, because it's something I've been noticing myself and it's been bothering me quite a bit. I've always been a very active person, you see. I like to keep busy. I have my book club that meets every other Thursday at the community center, and then there's the Friday night line dancing class—which, I know, sounds a bit silly for someone my age, but it's wonderful exercise and usually just such a hoot. And I still go. I make myself get dressed, I drive over there, I walk through the doors, and I sit in my usual chair or take my spot on the floor. 

But it's just not the same. It's the strangest feeling. I'm there in the room, people are laughing and talking about the chapters we read or trying to follow the instructor, and I just feel like... like I'm sitting behind a thick pane of glass. I can see it all happening, but I can't quite touch it or feel it. I'm just going through the motions. Even the things I do around the house, like tending to my garden—my roses are usually my pride and joy, I spend hours out there in the spring—or baking my lemon pound cake for the neighbors when they're under the weather... I still do those things, because that's what you do, isn't it? You keep up your responsibilities. But they don't give me that little spark anymore. That little lift in my chest that says, "Oh, I've done a good job," or "Isn't this a lovely afternoon." It's just... flat. Everything just feels terribly flat, no matter how hard I try to participate.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in?

Well, I... I've really been trying to find something, Doctor. I really have. Because when you realize that all the things you usually love are just leaving you cold, you think, well, I just need to try something else, or maybe I just need to try harder. 

But if I'm being completely honest, no, not really. It's just as I was saying, I still make myself show up for things like the book club or the dance night, because I've always believed that you can't just stop living your life, you know? You have to keep putting one foot in front of the other. But lately, I just sit there feeling like I'm behind that pane of glass I mentioned. I watch everyone else having a wonderful time, and I just feel... nothing. 

And it's the same with my quiet things at home. My garden, which usually brings me such peace... I go out there with my shears and my gloves, and I look at the roses, and I know they're beautiful, but I don't *feel* that they're beautiful. Even cooking for the neighbors, which has always been my way of showing I care... I'll bake the cake, I'll wrap it up nicely in foil with a little bow, I'll walk it over, and they're so appreciative, but it just doesn't give me that little lift it used to. It's almost like... like my capacity to feel joy has just been turned off like a faucet. I keep turning the handle, doing all the things I'm supposed to do, but nothing comes out. It's terribly discouraging, to be quite honest with you. Terribly discouraging.
Do you often feel guilty about things that have happened since your sister passed away?

Oh, doctor... guilt. Yes. That's... well, that's a word that has been rattling around in my head day and night lately. You know, when someone passes away, especially when it's so sudden like it was with her, you just can't help but rewind the tape. I'll sit in my armchair by the window—the one where I usually read, though as I mentioned, the reading just hasn't been happening much—and I just replay those last few weeks over and over and over again. 

I keep going over that time with my sister, dissecting every little interaction we had. I tell myself, 'Why didn't I call her on that Wednesday?' We almost always talked in the evenings, but I think I was tired one night and just didn't pick up the phone, and now I just agonize over it. I tell myself I should have called more. I should have listened better when she was talking about her day, instead of just half-listening while I was wiping down the kitchen counters. I just keep thinking I should have done something more useful, been a better sister in those final days, made sure she knew exactly how much she meant to me. 

And the frustrating part is, the rational side of my brain—the side that earned a degree and knows how the world works—that part of me knows perfectly well that I couldn't have changed what happened. An extra phone call wouldn't have stopped her from passing away. I know that. I really do. But the heart doesn't listen to reason, does it? It just sits there and aches and tells you all the ways you fell short. I just keep finding myself apologizing to her in my head, thinking if I had just paid closer attention, maybe... well, I don't know what maybe. It's just a terrible, heavy feeling to carry around, constantly second-guessing every conversation we had at those Tuesday lunches.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your sister passed away?

Well, I haven't really been tracking it on a scale, Doctor, mostly because I've never been one to obsess over numbers like that. But my clothes... yes, they are definitely fitting a bit looser these days. My favorite navy slacks, the ones I always wear to the book club because they're so comfortable and they have those nice deep pockets? I had to pull out a belt for them just last week, which I haven't done in years. 

It's not that I'm trying to lose weight, mind you. At my age, you know you're supposed to keep your strength up, and I've always enjoyed cooking, as I mentioned with the baking. But lately, it's just... food just doesn't call to me much anymore. It's the strangest thing. I used to wake up and think about what I might make for dinner, maybe plan a nice little roast or a chicken casserole, perhaps look through some of my old recipe cards. Now, the whole idea of planning a meal, preparing it, eating it... it just feels exhausting. 

So, I'll go into the kitchen around lunchtime, and I'll think I should eat, but nothing sounds good. I'll just fix a little piece of toast, maybe with a scrape of butter, or heat up half a can of soup—just chicken noodle, nothing fancy. And then I'll sit down, take a few bites, and I'm just done. I'll wrap the rest up and put it in the fridge, thinking I'll finish it later, but then evening rolls around, and I realize I've barely eaten a thing all day. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, even brought over a lovely shepherd's pie on Tuesday—bless her heart, she knows I've been struggling—and I felt terrible because I barely managed two spoonfuls before I had to put it away. It just feels like too much effort to eat, really.
Do you find yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

Moving slowly? Well... let me think about that for a moment, Doctor. I don't... no, I don't believe so. I mean, obviously, I'm sixty-nine years old, so I'm certainly not sprinting up the stairs or rushing around the house the way I did when I was in my thirties, or even my fifties for that matter. But as far as an actual change recently? No, I wouldn't say I'm moving any slower than my usual pace. 

It's funny you ask, because I was actually just noticing this the other day. When I get up to make my morning tea—I always have a cup of Earl Grey first thing, it's a habit I picked up years ago because coffee just became a bit too harsh on my stomach—anyway, when I walk into the kitchen to put the kettle on, my body seems to move at the exact same clip it always has. I still wipe down the counters with the same brisk motions, I still fold the laundry at the same speed. It's like... well, the engine is still running at the exact same pace, you see? It's just that, as I mentioned before, I don't really have the desire to do these things, but when I force myself to do them, my hands and my legs do exactly what they're told, right when they're told to do it. 

And as for reacting... well, just yesterday morning, the mail carrier, Mr. Henderson—he's been doing our neighborhood route for nearly a decade now, lovely man, always waves—he dropped a rather heavy package on the front porch and it made quite a sudden thud. I was sitting in my armchair, and I jumped up and turned around to look out the window just as quick as you please. I didn't feel sluggish or delayed at all. So, no, physically speaking, I don't feel like I'm moving through molasses or anything of that sort. Everything physical seems to be operating on its normal schedule, for whatever that's worth.
Do you feel like you're restless or fidgety, or do you have an inner feeling of agitation?

Restless? Agitated? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, if anything, it's quite the opposite. I mean, I don't feel like I have the energy to be restless, if that makes any sense. You know, when I think of someone being fidgety, I think of my grandson, little Leo—well, he's not so little anymore, he just turned twelve last month, but when he was younger, he simply couldn't sit still for a family dinner. He'd be tapping his fork, swinging his legs under the table, constantly looking around like he was waiting for a starting pistol to go off. My daughter was always telling him, "Leo, please, just for five minutes, settle down." 

But me? No, I don't have that sort of energy coursing through me. I don't feel like I need to pace the floors or wring my hands. As I was saying earlier about sitting in my armchair by the window, I can sit there for hours on end. I just sort of... settle into the cushions and stay put. I don't feel this urge to get up and do something, or like my skin is crawling, or any kind of nervous tension like that. 

I suppose the closest thing to agitation I feel is just that heavy sadness we talked about, the guilt and the thoughts just turning over and over in my mind, but physically? No. I don't find myself tapping my foot or needing to move about. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins—the one who brought the shepherd's pie—she's a bit of a fidgeter. Whenever we sit on the porch for a chat, she's always adjusting her sweater, or smoothing her skirt, or picking little pieces of lint off her sleeve. I watch her and it almost makes me tired just seeing how much she moves while she's supposedly relaxing. But I don't do any of that. I just sit quite still, really. So no, Doctor, no restlessness or agitation to speak of. Just... stillness, mostly.
Do you feel sad most of the day, nearly every day?

Sad most of the day? Oh, well... no. No, I wouldn't really say that. I know we've talked about how heavy things feel, and the guilt, but it's not exactly a constant sadness, if you see what I mean. It's not like I wake up and immediately start crying and cry all day long until I go to sleep. 

In fact, the mornings are usually quite alright. When I first wake up and have my Earl Grey tea—like I mentioned, out in the kitchen—I'll often look out the window at the garden. I have these beautiful hydrangeas that my late husband planted, the big blue ones, and they're just starting to bloom. When I see them, I feel a little spark of... well, not joy, exactly, but a quiet sort of contentment. I can appreciate that they're lovely. And sometimes, if the weather is nice, I'll sit out on the patio with my tea and watch the birds at the feeder. We get cardinals, mostly, and the occasional blue jay, though they can be quite bossy with the smaller birds. In those moments, I don't feel overwhelmingly sad. I just feel... present, I suppose.

It's really only when my mind starts wandering back to my sister, or when I look at the clock and realize I haven't done anything productive, that the heavy feeling creeps back in. But it comes and goes. Yesterday, for instance, I spent a good hour on the phone with my daughter, talking about Leo's upcoming baseball tournament. She was telling me all about how they have to travel three states over, and the logistics of getting all his gear packed, and I was actually quite engaged in the conversation. I didn't feel sad at all while we were talking. It was only after we hung up, and the house was quiet again, that I felt a bit low. 

So, it's certainly not an all-day, every-day kind of thing. It's more like... patches of clouds, you know? Sometimes the sun is out, and sometimes it's overcast, but it's not a constant downpour. I have moments where I feel perfectly fine, or at least neutral. It's just that the quiet moments seem to invite those guilty thoughts, but I wouldn't describe my days as being filled with sadness from morning till night.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities that you used to find pleasurable?

Lost interest? Well... I suppose that’s a slightly complicated question, Doctor, because it’s not that I’ve stopped doing things altogether. I haven't just shut myself in a dark room, if that's what you mean. I still go through the motions of my routine. 

For instance, my Tuesday afternoon book club. I’ve been going to that for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We usually meet at the local library, though sometimes we gather at my friend Eleanor’s house if the weather is frightful. We're reading this historical fiction novel right now, set in 1920s London, which normally is exactly the sort of thing I would just devour in a single weekend. And I still make myself show up for it. I sit in my usual chair, I even bake my lemon drizzle cake to bring along, just like always. And it's the same with the Thursday dance night at the community center. My husband and I used to go every single week, and I kept it up after he passed because the music is so wonderful, all the old big band tunes, and it's good exercise. I still force myself to go to that, too. 

But the thing is... lately, when I’m sitting there, surrounded by my friends discussing the chapters, or when I'm at the community center listening to the band tune up, I just feel like... well, like I'm sitting behind a thick pane of glass. I can see everyone laughing and chatting and having a marvelous time, and I know I should be feeling that same warmth and excitement, but the feeling just doesn't reach me on the other side of that glass. I’m physically present, but I’m not really participating in the joy of it, if that makes any sense. 

And it’s the exact same way with the things I do around the house. I mentioned my garden earlier, and how I can appreciate that the hydrangeas are lovely to look at. But it used to be that getting my hands in the dirt, pruning the bushes, or seeing the first blooms of the season would give me such a thrill. A real sense of accomplishment. Or cooking for the neighbors—I used to absolutely love making a big batch of blueberry muffins or putting together a nice casserole for someone if they were feeling under the weather, just to see the smile on their face when I dropped it off. But now, even my garden and cooking for the neighbors... they just don't give me that little lift they used to. I still do them, because the weeds need pulling and people appreciate a home-cooked meal, but the actual pleasure I used to draw from those activities seems to have just evaporated. It’s terribly frustrating, to be perfectly honest with you, to do all the things you love and feel absolutely nothing in return.
For how long have you felt like you're just going through the motions of your daily activities without really enjoying them?

How long... well, let me think about that for a moment. It is funny how time sort of blurs together when you are just going through the motions, isn't it? You lose track of the days because Tuesday feels exactly like Thursday. But I suppose if I really sit down and pinpoint exactly when that pane of glass came down between me and the rest of the world, it has been right around a month now. Yes, just about exactly a month. 

You see, that was when my sister passed away. And it was just so terribly unexpected, Doctor. Completely out of the blue. We were very close, we talked on the telephone every single Sunday evening without fail, and she was always so vibrant. One minute she was perfectly fine, telling me all about the new curtains she was sewing for her guest room, and the next, I am getting a dreadful phone call from her husband. I can still remember exactly where I was standing in the kitchen, holding my favorite blue tea towel, when he told me. It was such a profound shock. You simply do not prepare yourself for something like that when someone has always been so full of life. 

And ever since then, since that awful week, that is when this feeling really settled in. I went to the funeral, of course, and I helped her husband organize the reception because he was just completely beside himself, poor man. I did all the things I was supposed to do, arranged the flowers and the catering and all of that. But coming back home to my own empty house after all that was over... that is when I realized the joy had just completely seeped out of my routine. So, yes, it has been about a month, right since she died so suddenly, that I have been feeling this way.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite since your sister passed away?

Appetite... yes, well, that’s another thing that has just sort of slipped away, I suppose. I used to be quite the planner when it came to meals, you know. I’d sit down on a Sunday with my recipe boxes—the little wooden ones my late husband made for me—and I would plan out a proper dinner for every night of the week. Even after he passed, I kept it up. I’d make a nice piece of baked salmon on Tuesdays, maybe a small roast chicken on Sundays so I'd have leftovers for lunch. 

But lately, especially since everything happened with my sister... food just doesn't call to me much anymore. It’s the strangest thing. I’ll walk into the kitchen and open the refrigerator door, and I'll just stand there staring at the shelves, and absolutely nothing looks appealing. So I just close the door again. Eventually, I'll think to myself that I really ought to put something in my stomach, so I'll fix a little toast—just with a scrape of butter, maybe some marmalade if I can manage it—or I'll heat up a small bowl of soup. Just a simple tomato soup from a can, nothing fussy. 

And I'll have that at the kitchen table, and then the whole day will just slip by. I'll be puttering around the house, or looking out at the garden like I told you, and suddenly it's evening, the sun is going down, and I'll realize I've barely eaten a single thing all day long. And it's certainly not on purpose, Doctor. Goodness knows, at my age, I am not trying to lose weight or go on any sort of silly diet. I’ve always been perfectly content with my figure. It’s just that the hunger simply isn't there to remind me. My daughter actually came over the other day and gave me a bit of a scolding because she saw how full the pantry was with groceries I hadn't touched since her last visit. I had to tell her that I just can't seem to muster the desire to cook a full meal when even a slice of bread feels like a chore to get through...
Have you lost more than 5% of your body weight since your sister passed away?

Five percent? Oh, well... let me think about the math on that for a second. I suppose I usually hover right around 140 pounds, give or take a pound or two depending on the season. I've been at that weight for years and years. But, as I was just saying a moment ago, since food just doesn't call to me much anymore, the pounds have certainly started slipping away. 

I stepped on the scale in my bathroom just the other morning—it's one of those older dial ones, not the fancy digital kind my daughter has, but it's always been very reliable—and I saw I was down to about 130. So... yes, I suppose that is more than five percent, isn't it? Nearly ten pounds in just a month. It really is just because I'll fix that little piece of toast or a cup of soup, like I mentioned, and then I'll just get lost in my thoughts, and I'll realize by evening I've barely eaten a single thing all day long. 

And I really must emphasize again, even though the scale is going down, I'm absolutely not trying to lose weight. I was perfectly happy with my figure just the way it was. But now my everyday slacks are getting awfully loose around the waist. I actually had to dig out a brown leather belt from the back of my closet—one I haven't worn in at least a decade—just to keep my trousers up when I went out to check on the hydrangeas the other day. It's just a consequence of having no desire to eat, I suppose, rather than any sort of intentional diet.
Do you feel like your thoughts are slowed down, or that it takes you longer than usual to think through things?

Slowed down... oh, goodness, yes. It is exactly like that. Like wading through molasses, Doctor. Just thick and sticky and exhausting. I have always prided myself on being sharp, you know. I kept the books for my late husband's business for nearly thirty years, so I am very used to numbers and reading and keeping everything perfectly organized. But lately... well, it is just so terribly frustrating. 

Just the other afternoon, I was trying to sit down and do my monthly finances. My grandson, bless his heart, set me up with one of those budgeting spreadsheets on the computer a few years ago. He color-coded the whole thing for me, very clever, to make it easy to track my utility bills and groceries. But now, I will open it up, and I'll stare at the same budgeting spreadsheet for what feels like an hour, and the numbers just sort of float there. I can't make head or tail of them. 

And it is not just the numbers, either. I attend this little community workshop on Wednesday mornings—well, I try to attend, it's a sort of local history and gardening group at the library—and we occasionally have these short reading materials to go over beforehand. I found myself sitting in my armchair with the handout, and I swear to you, I will reread a paragraph for the workshop three or four times and still not take in what it says. It is as if the connection between my eyes and my brain has just completely frayed. I look at the words, I know perfectly well they are English, but the meaning just slips right through my fingers. 

And then, of course, I start worrying about why I can't understand it, which only makes it harder to focus! It feels like I have to force my brain to turn the gears, and they are all just rusted shut. It takes me twice as long to do the simplest little tasks now because my mind just keeps wandering off into this sort of foggy blankness, and I have to start the whole thought process over again from the very beginning.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual, or is it more of a lack of motivation that's holding you back from doing things?

Moving slowly? No, I wouldn't say I'm physically moving any slower. I mean, my joints are a bit stiff in the mornings, but that's just arthritis, and I've had that for years. It's not like my body is refusing to work, or that I'm dragging my feet when I walk. I can still get up from my chair just fine, and I can walk out to the garden at a perfectly normal pace. 

It's really just the motivation, Doctor. The desire to actually *do* the things. Like I was saying about the cooking, and even just getting dressed sometimes. I'll wake up, and I know I should get out of bed, I know I should go make a cup of tea and start the day, but the thought of it just feels so overwhelmingly pointless. I just don't have the drive to start the engine, so to speak. So I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about all the things I ought to be doing, but I just can't bring myself to care enough to actually do them. It's a terrible feeling, really, knowing you're capable of doing something but just not having the willpower to make it happen.
Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or had a loss of interest in activities most of the day?

Well, two weeks... oh, it's been much longer than that, Doctor. It really has. Ever since my sister passed, it's just been this constant, heavy cloud. And as for losing interest, yes, absolutely. It's exactly as you say. 

I've always been such a busybody, you know? Always out and about. I still make myself show up for things, because I know I'm supposed to. Like my Tuesday evening book club—we've been meeting for nearly fifteen years, and we're reading this fascinating biography of Eleanor Roosevelt right now, or at least, everyone else thinks it's fascinating. And the Thursday night community center dance, which I've always loved. But lately, when I go... I just sit there. I sit there in my usual chair, and people are talking and laughing and discussing the book or the music, and I just feel like I'm sitting behind a thick pane of glass. I can see them, I can hear them, but I'm completely disconnected from it all. I'm just going through the motions. 

And it's the same with the things I do around the house. My garden, for instance. I've always taken such pride in my hydrangeas and my prize-winning tomatoes—I even won a ribbon at the county fair for them back in 2018. Usually, getting my hands in the dirt and seeing the first little green shoots of spring would just fill me with such joy. And cooking! I used to love baking casseroles or making a fresh batch of blueberry muffins for the neighbors when someone was sick or just had a new baby. But now... I look at the garden, and it just looks like work. I think about baking, and I just can't summon the energy or the care. Even when I do manage to do something, it doesn't give me that little lift it used to. It's just flat. Everything is just so awfully flat and gray, all day long.
Have you felt like a burden to your family or friends since your sister passed away?

A burden? Well... I suppose I try very hard not to be. I don't want to be a bother to anyone, especially my grandson, he's so busy with his own life and his new job at the firm. But... oh, Doctor, it's not so much feeling like a burden to them right now, it's more this terrible, heavy feeling I carry around about my sister. 

I just... I can't seem to stop my mind from going in circles about it. I sit in my chair, the one by the window where I used to call her every Sunday afternoon, and I just keep going over and over those last few weeks before she passed. I play it all back like a film reel in my head. I keep telling myself I should have called her more often. I should have called on Wednesdays, too, not just Sundays. And when we did talk, I should have listened better. I remember one time she mentioned being unusually tired, and I just brushed it off as us getting older—we used to joke about our creaky bones, you see—and I think, why didn't I press her on it? Why didn't I tell her to see a doctor right then? 

I just feel this awful, gnawing sense that I should have done something more useful. Maybe gone over there and helped her around the house, or cooked some meals for her freezer so she wouldn't have to stand at the stove. I know, logically, in the back of my mind... I know I couldn't have changed what happened. It was a heart attack, and the doctors said it was very sudden. Part of me knows I couldn't have stopped it. But I just feel so useless, so entirely guilty that I wasn't a better sister at the very end. It just eats away at me, day and night, this feeling that I failed her when she might have needed me most.
Have you had any days in the past month where you didn't feel depressed or disconnected from activities?

Well... no, Doctor, I really haven't. Not a single day, if I'm being perfectly honest. It's just been one long, gray stretch. And, well, I know exactly when it started, too. It's been about a month now. Yes, a month... ever since Mary passed. 

It was all so sudden, you see. So completely unexpected. One day she was perfectly fine, or at least, she seemed perfectly fine when we spoke on the phone, and then... then she was just gone. And ever since that phone call, the one from her neighbor, Mrs. Higgins—lovely woman, really, she's the one who found her—ever since that moment, it's just been this constant, heavy feeling. I haven't had a single morning where I woke up and felt like myself, or felt like doing anything at all. It's just been this solid month of feeling completely disconnected from everything I used to care about, just dragging myself through the days because I have to, but never actually feeling... alive, I suppose. Just a whole month of this grayness since she died.
Have you had any thoughts of self-harm or suicide since your sister passed away, even if you didn't intend to act on them?

Oh... well, that is a very difficult thing to say out loud. I've never been the sort of person to think such things, Doctor. Never. Even when my husband passed away back in 2004, God rest his soul, I was terribly sad, of course, but I never had thoughts quite like this. 

But lately... since Mary died... it's the mornings that are just so impossibly hard. I wake up, and I see the sunlight coming through the floral curtains in my bedroom—the ones Mary actually helped me pick out at Macy's years and years ago—and before I even swing my legs over the side of the bed, this terrible, crushing weight just drops right onto my chest. And I catch myself thinking... I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I simply hadn't woken up at all. If I could have just stayed asleep and not had to face another long, empty day without her. 

It's not that I want to do anything violent to myself. I really don't. I don't have any sort of plan to hurt myself or do anything drastic, I promise you that. I couldn't bear to put my grandson through that kind of shock, not with his new job and everything he has going on. But just... wishing I could slip away quietly in my sleep, just wishing the Lord would take me so I wouldn't have to feel this grayness anymore. It happens so often now, these mornings where I just lie there thinking how much simpler it would be to just not be here. And honestly, Doctor, that is exactly what scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and ask for help. Because it's just not like me at all to think that way, and it frightened me to realize how often I was wishing I just wouldn't wake up.

And then, of course, I start worrying about why I can't understand it, which only makes it harder to focus! It feels like I have to force my brain to turn the gears, and they are all just rusted shut. It takes me twice as long to do the simplest little tasks now because my mind just keeps wandering off into this sort of foggy blankness, and I have to start the whole thought process over again from the very beginning.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation to differentiate between F33.0 and F33.1
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual, or is it more of a lack of motivation that's holding you back from doing things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving more slowly than usual), which corresponds to a symptom not present in the patient's profile (S028).

patient.answer:
Moving slowly? No, I wouldn't say I'm physically moving any slower. I mean, my joints are a bit stiff in the mornings, but that's just arthritis, and I've had that for years. It's not like my body is refusing to work, or that I'm dragging my feet when I walk. I can still get up from my chair just fine, and I can walk out to the garden at a perfectly normal pace. 

It's really just the motivation, Doctor. The desire to actually *do* the things. Like I was saying about the cooking, and even just getting dressed sometimes. I'll wake up, and I know I should get out of bed, I know I should go make a cup of tea and start the day, but the thought of it just feels so overwhelmingly pointless. I just don't have the drive to start the engine, so to speak. So I'll just lie there, staring at the ceiling, thinking about all the things I ought to be doing, but I just can't bring myself to care enough to actually do them. It's a terrible feeling, really, knowing you're capable of doing something but just not having the willpower to make it happen.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or had a loss of interest in activities most of the day?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I still make myself show up for things like book club or the dance night, but lately I sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass, and even my garden and cooking for the neighbors don't give me that little lift they used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a loss of interest in activities most of the day, which directly corresponds to the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, two weeks... oh, it's been much longer than that, Doctor. It really has. Ever since my sister passed, it's just been this constant, heavy cloud. And as for losing interest, yes, absolutely. It's exactly as you say. 

I've always been such a busybody, you know? Always out and about. I still make myself show up for things, because I know I'm supposed to. Like my Tuesday evening book club—we've been meeting for nearly fifteen years, and we're reading this fascinating biography of Eleanor Roosevelt right now, or at least, everyone else thinks it's fascinating. And the Thursday night community center dance, which I've always loved. But lately, when I go... I just sit there. I sit there in my usual chair, and people are talking and laughing and discussing the book or the music, and I just feel like I'm sitting behind a thick pane of glass. I can see them, I can hear them, but I'm completely disconnected from it all. I'm just going through the motions. 

And it's the same with the things I do around the house. My garden, for instance. I've always taken such pride in my hydrangeas and my prize-winning tomatoes—I even won a ribbon at the county fair for them back in 2018. Usually, getting my hands in the dirt and seeing the first little green shoots of spring would just fill me with such joy. And cooking! I used to love baking casseroles or making a fresh batch of blueberry muffins for the neighbors when someone was sick or just had a new baby. But now... I look at the garden, and it just looks like work. I think about baking, and I just can't summon the energy or the care. Even when I do manage to do something, it doesn't give me that little lift it used to. It's just flat. Everything is just so awfully flat and gray, all day long.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you felt like a burden to your family or friends since your sister passed away?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over the last weeks with my sister and telling myself I should have called more, listened better, done something more useful, even when part of me knows I couldn't have changed what happened.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel like a burden to my family or friends, which is a common manifestation of feelings of worthlessness or guilt.

patient.answer:
A burden? Well... I suppose I try very hard not to be. I don't want to be a bother to anyone, especially my grandson, he's so busy with his own life and his new job at the firm. But... oh, Doctor, it's not so much feeling like a burden to them right now, it's more this terrible, heavy feeling I carry around about my sister. 

I just... I can't seem to stop my mind from going in circles about it. I sit in my chair, the one by the window where I used to call her every Sunday afternoon, and I just keep going over and over those last few weeks before she passed. I play it all back like a film reel in my head. I keep telling myself I should have called her more often. I should have called on Wednesdays, too, not just Sundays. And when we did talk, I should have listened better. I remember one time she mentioned being unusually tired, and I just brushed it off as us getting older—we used to joke about our creaky bones, you see—and I think, why didn't I press her on it? Why didn't I tell her to see a doctor right then? 

I just feel this awful, gnawing sense that I should have done something more useful. Maybe gone over there and helped her around the house, or cooked some meals for her freezer so she wouldn't have to stand at the stove. I know, logically, in the back of my mind... I know I couldn't have changed what happened. It was a heart attack, and the doctors said it was very sudden. Part of me knows I couldn't have stopped it. But I just feel so useless, so entirely guilty that I wasn't a better sister at the very end. It just eats away at me, day and night, this feeling that I failed her when she might have needed me most.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's depression is persistent
doctor.question: Have you had any days in the past month where you didn't feel depressed or disconnected from activities?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a month, since my sister died unexpectedly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the consistency and timeline of the symptoms over the past month, which corresponds to the duration of the current depressive episode.

patient.answer:
Well... no, Doctor, I really haven't. Not a single day, if I'm being perfectly honest. It's just been one long, gray stretch. And, well, I know exactly when it started, too. It's been about a month now. Yes, a month... ever since Mary passed. 

It was all so sudden, you see. So completely unexpected. One day she was perfectly fine, or at least, she seemed perfectly fine when we spoke on the phone, and then... then she was just gone. And ever since that phone call, the one from her neighbor, Mrs. Higgins—lovely woman, really, she's the one who found her—ever since that moment, it's just been this constant, heavy feeling. I haven't had a single morning where I woke up and felt like myself, or felt like doing anything at all. It's just been this solid month of feeling completely disconnected from everything I used to care about, just dragging myself through the days because I have to, but never actually feeling... alive, I suppose. Just a whole month of this grayness since she died.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal thoughts without a plan
doctor.question: Have you had any thoughts of self-harm or suicide since your sister passed away, even if you didn't intend to act on them?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: What scared me enough to ask for help is that I keep having mornings where I think it might be easier if I just didn't wake up, even though I don't have a plan to hurt myself.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thoughts of self-harm or suicide, which directly corresponds to the Death_Suicide symptom.

patient.answer:
Oh... well, that is a very difficult thing to say out loud. I've never been the sort of person to think such things, Doctor. Never. Even when my husband passed away back in 2004, God rest his soul, I was terribly sad, of course, but I never had thoughts quite like this. 

But lately... since Mary died... it's the mornings that are just so impossibly hard. I wake up, and I see the sunlight coming through the floral curtains in my bedroom—the ones Mary actually helped me pick out at Macy's years and years ago—and before I even swing my legs over the side of the bed, this terrible, crushing weight just drops right onto my chest. And I catch myself thinking... I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I simply hadn't woken up at all. If I could have just stayed asleep and not had to face another long, empty day without her. 

It's not that I want to do anything violent to myself. I really don't. I don't have any sort of plan to hurt myself or do anything drastic, I promise you that. I couldn't bear to put my grandson through that kind of shock, not with his new job and everything he has going on. But just... wishing I could slip away quietly in my sleep, just wishing the Lord would take me so I wouldn't have to feel this grayness anymore. It happens so often now, these mornings where I just lie there thinking how much simpler it would be to just not be here. And honestly, Doctor, that is exactly what scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and ask for help. Because it's just not like me at all to think that way, and it frightened me to realize how often I was wishing I just wouldn't wake up.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of depressed mood, loss of interest in activities, significant weight loss, and recurrent thoughts of death, which have been present for about a month since the patient's sister passed away, are consistent with a Major Depressive Disorder. The presence of a significant depressive episode with a clear precipitating factor (the sister's death) and a duration of more than two weeks supports this diagnosis.
